opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the community's views have shifted a lot over the past year or so.

The skeptical take is that RL doesn't teach the model anything fundamentally new. Pre-training puts all the latent capability in there, and RL just sharpens the distribution. It takes something the model could do one time in a hundred and makes it do that reliably. There's evidence for this: if you look at pass@k with very large k, the base model can sometimes match or beat the RL'd model, which suggests the capability was already there.

But I think that framing undersells what's happening. First, reliability is itself a new capability in a very practical sense. A model that solves a hard problem one time in a thousand is useless for real work. A model that solves it nine times in ten is transformative. Going from "theoretically possible if you sample enough" to "dependable" is most of the difference between a toy and something that does economically useful work.

Second, and more importantly, once you start doing RL on long-horizon tasks, you're composing skills in ways that almost never appear in pre-training data. Nobody writes down the full trace of an engineer debugging a gnarly distributed systems problem over six hours, with all the dead ends and the "wait, that's wrong, let me back up." That's not on the internet. So the model has to learn it by doing, by getting a reward signal when it succeeds. And we're seeing that with enough compute and a clean enough signal, models genuinely learn new things through RL. The constraint has mostly been that we weren't spending much compute on RL compared to pre-training.

The way I think about it, pre-training gives you an incredibly rich prior: a model of the world, of language, of how people reason. RL is where you teach it to act on that prior, to pursue a goal, notice its own mistakes, and keep going. The prior matters enormously, because RL with a weak prior is hopeless; you never get any reward signal to learn from. But given a strong enough base, RL can take you a long way past what was explicitly in the data.

The real bottleneck now is less "can RL teach new things" and more "can we build environments and reward signals that are rich and verifiable enough." Where we have clean feedback, like competitive programming or math, we've seen superhuman-level performance emerge. The open question is how far that extends to fuzzier domains where it's harder to say what "correct" looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says RL has received less compute than pre-training and depends on a strong pre-training prior, but does not state that pre-training is likely more learning-efficient.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says models can “genuinely learn new things through RL” and describes learning long-horizon skills by doing.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that pre-training’s next-token prediction objective could be reformulated as an RL task.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that pre-training and RL are doing different jobs, and the confusion comes from treating them as competing ways to get the same thing.

Pre-training is where the model acquires its representation of the world. You're compressing an enormous corpus, and in doing so the model learns concepts, facts, how code works, how arguments are structured. It's broad and it's dense in signal. Every token is supervision. But what it teaches you is roughly "what does text like this look like," not "how do I achieve this outcome."

RL is sparse by comparison. You get a reward at the end of a long trajectory, maybe a single bit. So on a per-sample basis you're learning far less about the world. What you're learning is how to steer. Which of the things the model already sort of knows should it actually deploy, in what order, with what kind of persistence, when it's trying to accomplish something. That's a very different kind of knowledge, and it turns out to matter enormously for things like long-horizon agentic work, where the gap between "knows the relevant facts" and "actually gets to the end of the task" is huge.

The question people really want answered is whether RL can teach genuinely new capabilities or whether it's just eliciting what's latent. I've come to think that framing is a little too clean. Early on, when the compute going into RL was tiny relative to pre-training, it looked a lot like elicitation. You could get a big jump in, say, math by sharpening behaviors the model was already capable of. But as you scale RL compute up to something comparable to pre-training, that stops being a sufficient explanation. The model is learning strategies that weren't in the pre-training distribution in any meaningful sense, because nobody writes down the process of trying something, failing, and backing up in the way the model ends up doing it. Those behaviors are discovered through interaction with the environment, and they get consolidated into the weights.

So I'd say: pre-training gives you the prior, RL gives you the policy. And the thing that has surprised people, including me, is how far you can push the policy once you have a strong enough prior to search over. The constraint right now is less about whether RL can teach new things and more about whether you can build environments and reward signals rich enough for it to learn them.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s dense signal (“Every token is supervision”) with RL’s sparse reward and says RL teaches less about the world per sample, communicating greater learning efficiency for pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says that at sufficient scale RL teaches strategies not meaningfully present in the pre-training distribution, discovered through environmental interaction and consolidated into the model’s weights.

r003.rationale: It does not state that pre-training’s next-token prediction objective could be reformulated as an RL task.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is less clean than people sometimes make it. Pre-training gives the model an enormous amount of knowledge, along with patterns for how to reason and act. Reinforcement learning then gives it a way to discover which of those patterns actually work—and potentially to build new strategies through trial and error.

There’s an argument that RL can only bring out capabilities that were already in the model, because you have to sample a successful answer before you can reinforce it. But I don’t think that establishes a hard limit. Imagine the model occasionally gets one step right. You reinforce that, and now it reaches the next step more often, which gives it an opportunity to learn something it almost never would have discovered before. Over many iterations, you can end up with behavior that was vanishingly unlikely under the original model.

The important question is whether your training environment supports that process. Can you reliably tell when the model has made progress? Is there enough exploration? Are the problems at the right difficulty? If you only reward answers on a fixed set of easy problems, you might mostly make existing capabilities more reliable. If you have a rich environment with progressively harder problems and good feedback, there’s much more room for learning.

So I’d think of pre-training as providing a very powerful starting point. The extent to which RL can take you beyond it is an empirical question, rather than something you can settle by saying the successful trajectory had to have nonzero probability beforehand.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training as a powerful starting point but does not say it is more learning-efficient than reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can build new strategies through trial and error and can take the model beyond its pre-trained capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that pre-training’s next-token prediction objective could be reformulated as a reinforcement learning task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is less sharp than people sometimes make it out to be. Pre-training gives you this enormous collection of representations and behaviors, and reinforcement learning gives you a way to select and build on those through interaction with an environment.

There’s a view that RL can only bring out capabilities that are already there. In a weak sense, that’s true: you need some probability of discovering a useful action before you can reinforce it. But that doesn’t mean the model has to be able to solve the entire problem at the start. It can learn one step, which makes a second step discoverable, and so on. The distribution you’re training on changes as the model improves. That’s how you can get beyond simply selecting the best answers from the original model.

The practical question is whether you have an environment where that process works. Can you verify success? Can the model explore enough to find something useful? Is the feedback informative enough? In a domain like coding, you can run the code and get feedback, so there’s a plausible route to learning through repeated attempts. In a domain where judging the answer is as hard as producing it, that’s much more difficult.

So I wouldn’t think of pre-training as teaching capabilities and RL as merely teaching the model to use them. Both can teach capabilities. They have different strengths, and the interesting question is how far we can push learning from experience once we have a sufficiently good starting point.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training and RL have different strengths, but does not present pre-training as more learning-efficient.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says both methods can teach capabilities and explains how RL can build new capabilities through iterative learning.

r003.rationale: It does not say that pre-training’s next-token prediction objective could be reformulated as an RL task.
